content: To ensure unbiased results, it is essential to include all relevant data in the analysis. To identify individuals with specific outcomes, we will use the planned treatment duration as recorded in many datasets. However, in cases where the planned duration is not provided, we will analyze the frequency distribution of treatment durations among patients successfully treated at the same centers. If the distribution is unimodal, the mode will be considered the planned duration. If the distribution is more complex, we will predict the duration based on key predictors such as age, extent of drug resistance, extent of disease, and specific drugs used at that center. Before analyzing each research question, we will conduct a descriptive analysis of the BPaL regimen and four comparator groups. This analysis will examine key characteristics such as age (both as a continuous variable and in specific age groups), sex, HIV status, extent of drug resistance, and country of treatment. This will help identify systematic differences between individuals receiving each regimen and potential differences in outcomes based on where the regimens were used. The findings from this analysis will inform further adjustments, including matching variables and the addition of random effects for the country of treatment. For each research question, the variables included in the analysis will be pre-specified but may be modified based on data completeness and availability. Sensitivity analyses may also be conducted to include or exclude additional variables based on the results of the descriptive analysis. The descriptive analysis will also determine the number of individuals included or excluded due to regimen composition. The four comparator groups are as follows: 1. Regimens containing bedaquiline (Bdq) and linezolid (Lzd) with other drugs. 2. Regimens containing Bdq with other drugs but not Lzd. 3. Regimens containing Lzd with other drugs but not Bdq. 4. Regimens containing neither Bdq nor Lzd. The primary comparisons will focus on relapse-free treatment success (defined as cure or treatment completion) versus bacteriological/clinical failure, relapse, or death. Additional comparisons will include relapse-free success versus death alone and relapse-free success versus a combination of failure, relapse, death, or loss to follow-up. To minimize bias and confounding, we will use a combination of exact matching and propensity score-based matching on several covariates to select comparator groups from the individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis. This matching will ensure that the comparator groups are as comparable as possible to the patients who received the BPaL regimen. The matching algorithm will randomly select the best matches without including outcome data. Variables for exact matching will depend on the distribution of characteristics in the Nix-TB data and will be finalized after detailed exploration. Critical variables for matching include: 1. Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB versus non-responsive/intolerant multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB. 2. HIV infection and antiretroviral therapy (ART) use. If exact matching cannot be achieved, propensity score matching will be used, incorporating variables such as age, sex, and other important predictors. Matching will be performed with replacement, and the success of matching will be assessed by evaluating the balance of confounders between the groups. We will also determine how many patients were matched more than once to different patients in the Nix-TB cohort, which may require additional methods to control for the effects of non-independence and increased variance. Given the small number of patients in the Nix-TB study, the power of the analysis is limited. To enhance statistical power, we will match up to four controls from the IPD to each Nix-TB patient, provided there are sufficient suitable matches. Logistic regression using mixed models will be conducted for each outcome, including random intercepts for each matched pair and, if necessary, for the country of treatment. Adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals will be calculated. Binomial regression with fixed effects will also be used to calculate adjusted risk differences and their associated confidence intervals. For post-treatment relapse, we will first identify datasets in which this outcome was assessed and obtain information from study authors on methods of ascertainment, follow-up intensity, and duration. This will help determine the comparability of relapse outcomes with those in the Nix-TB study. If follow-up duration and timing of relapse are not available for all individuals or centers, we will present cumulative incidence of relapse as the proportion of patients relapsing out of the total number who successfully completed treatment. This analysis will be repeated for each of the four primary comparisons. For safety outcomes, we will describe the occurrence of Grade 3–5 adverse events (AEs), serious AEs, and AEs resulting in permanent discontinuation of at least one of the three component drugs of the Nix-TB regimen. Permanent discontinuation of a drug will be considered a drug-associated AE for the drug that was stopped. We will also investigate the effects of dose reduction. These safety outcomes will not be compared to the comparator groups due to differences in AE ascertainment methods across datasets. However, we suggest comparing AE rates in the Nix-TB study to those in the EndTB dataset, as both used systematic methods for AE assessment. Sensitivity analyses will include matching Nix-TB patients to IPD patients from specific subpopulations, such as South African cohorts, high-income countries, or studies with at least six months of post-treatment follow-up for relapse. These analyses aim to account for unique characteristics of patient populations and ensure comparability of outcomes. Limitations of the analysis include potential selection bias in the Nix-TB trial due to the lack of randomization and differences in loss to follow-up between Nix-TB and IPD patients. While exact and propensity score matching can reduce these biases, they cannot eliminate them entirely. Additionally, relapse was not systematically measured in most IPD studies, which may lead to underestimation of relapse rates. Differences in follow-up duration between Nix-TB and comparator groups may also bias results. To address these limitations, we will use systematic matching methods and sensitivity analyses to enhance the clinical utility of the findings.
